samples.text:
Environmental problems like global warming and pollution is becoming more serious every year. Some people think that new technology will solve these problems, while others think that people must change their lifestyle. I will discuss both opinions in this essay.

Many people believe technology is the answer. For example, electric cars do not produce smoke, and solar panels and wind turbines can make clean energy instead of coal. Scientists are also developing new ways to recycle plastic and to grow food with less water. People who agree with this view say that it is very difficult to ask everyone to change their habits, so it is better to invent machines which can do the job for us.

However, other people argue that technology is not enough. New technology is often expensive, and poor countries cannot afford it. Also, it takes a long time to develop, but the environment need help now. Moreover, even if we have electric cars, people still buy too many things, throw away food and fly on holiday many times in a year. If people do not change these habits, the problems will continue. Simple actions like using public transport, eating less meat and reuse bags can make a big different if millions of people do them.

In my opinion, both technology and changing lifestyle are necessary, but changing the way we live is more important. Technology can help, but it cannot work alone if people continue to waste resources.

To sum up, some people think technology will save the environment and others believe people must change their behaviour. I think we need both, but individuals must take more responsibility for there actions.

samples.text:
How humanity should respond to environmental damage is one of the defining questions of our time. Some are confident that technological innovation will provide the answers, whereas others argue that nothing less than a change in how people live will be effective. In my view, technology is essential but insufficient on its own.

Those who place their faith in technology can point to impressive progress. The cost of renewable energy such as solar and wind power has fallen dramatically, electric vehicles are becoming mainstream, and researchers are developing methods to capture carbon and produce food more efficiently. The attraction of this approach is that it does not require billions of people to give up comforts they value. Instead, it allows economies to keep growing while their environmental impact declines.

On the other hand, critics argue that relying on future inventions is a risky strategy. Many promising technologies are still expensive or years away from large-scale use, while the damage to ecosystems is happening now. Moreover, efficiency gains are often cancelled out by rising consumption: cars have become cleaner, for instance, but there are far more of them on the roads. Unless people reduce waste, buy fewer disposable products and rethink habits such as frequent flying, even the cleanest technology may simply allow us to consume more.

I believe the most realistic solution combines both approaches. Governments should invest heavily in green technology, but they also need to encourage lifestyle changes through measures such as better public transport and incentives for repairing rather than replacing goods. Technology can make sustainable choices easier, but people must still be willing to make it.

In conclusion, while new technology will undoubtedly play a major role in solving environmental problems, lasting change also depends on individuals adapting the way they live.
samples.why: Clear, consistent position · both views extended with relevant examples · logical progression with clear paragraph focus · good collocations (efficiency gains, large-scale use) · frequent error-free sentences with one pronoun slip.

samples.text:
Faced with mounting evidence of environmental decline, societies are divided over where the solution lies. Some believe that technological progress will eventually resolve the crisis, while others insist that meaningful change can only come from altering the way people live. Although both perspectives contain important truths, I would argue that neither is adequate without the other.

The optimism surrounding technology is not without foundation. In recent decades, renewable energy has become cheaper and more widely available, battery technology has improved considerably, and innovations in areas such as building insulation and precision farming have reduced waste. Crucially, technological solutions do not depend on persuading billions of individuals to sacrifice their comfort, which makes them politically and socially more achievable than widespread behavioural change. From this perspective, human ingenuity offers the most practical route to a sustainable future.

However, relying solely on innovation carries significant risks. Many of the most ambitious technologies remain unproven at scale, and waiting for them to mature may squander time that the planet does not have. There is also a well-documented tendency for efficiency gains to be offset by increased consumption: as products become cheaper and cleaner to run, people often simply use more of them. Without a shift in attitudes towards consumption, waste and travel, technology risks treating the symptoms of environmental damage rather than its underlying causes.

In my view, the two approaches are mutually reinforcing. Technology is most effective when it makes sustainable behaviour convenient, as affordable public transport or efficient home heating does, and lifestyle changes are easier to sustain when practical alternatives exist. Policy should therefore pursue both, funding research while also using regulation and incentives to discourage wasteful habits.

In conclusion, while technological advances are indispensable in tackling environmental problems, they cannot succeed in isolation. A genuine solution requires people to reconsider how they live, supported by innovations that make greener choices easier.
samples.why: Both views fully developed and evaluated · well-argued position that integrates the two sides · logical sequencing and cohesion · wide, precise vocabulary used naturally · wide range of accurate complex structures.
